title: Alberta health officials to provide update on soldiers wounded at CFB Wainwright

image.caption: The burned area of Canadian Forces Base Wainwright is seen in Alberta, Canada, Monday, Oct. 19, 2026. (Ty O'Neil/Associated Press)

blocks.text: More than a month after a deadly fire engulfed a training range at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, Alberta health officials are expected to provide an update on the soldiers still recovering from the flames.
22 service members hurt in the disaster remain in hospital, 7 in critical condition

Military officials have said that on the afternoon of Oct. 17, a low-burning grass fire flared suddenly in a fierce windstorm and rapidly advanced on soldiers involved in a training exercise at the base about 200 kilometres southeast of Edmonton.
Four soldiers were killed as the flames spread rapidly beyond the boundaries of the training area. A fifth soldier succumbed to his injuries in an Ontario hospital on Nov. 13.
For many of the service members who survived the fire, the injuries were life-altering.
As the training field was evacuated and the flames spread beyond the base, 39 people were initially taken to hospital, many with severe burns.

items: Family of injured Wainwright soldier holds bedside vigil in burn unit

blocks.text: Military officials said that as of Saturday, 22 Canadian Armed Forces members injured in the fire remained hospitalized in Alberta, British Columbia and Ontario.
Provincial health officials said that, as of Tuesday, 20 of the wounded were being cared for in Alberta hospitals, with seven listed in critical condition.

In a news conference starting at 11 a.m. MT Thursday, senior health officials, along with a specialized burn care physician, are expected to share insights on how Alberta hospitals responded to the disaster and have continued to care for the wounded.

items: Fifth soldier dead from injuries suffered in CFB Wainwright fire, officials say

blocks.text: In a statement Wednesday, officials said the news conference will provide insights on the initial response, from the role of rural health care teams in emergency response to the complex burn and trauma care that is supporting patients through their recovery.

Those expected to speak Thursday are Dr. Sayeh Zielke, interim CEO of Acute Care Alberta, Michael Suddes, interim COO of the Edmonton Corridor for Alberta Health Services, and Dr. Josh Wong, interim medical director of the Edmonton Firefighters' Burn Treatment Unit at the University of Alberta Hospital.
Prime Minister Mark Carney has described the fire as one of the worst tragedies for the Armed Forces on home soil during peacetime.

items: Canadian Armed Forces sending nurses to Alberta to help treat CFB Wainwright survivors

blocks.text: Three investigations are examining the circumstances of the fire, including the cause, spread and why the live-fire training exercise continued as fierce winds whipped the flames across the base.
Military officials have pledged to support the soldiers through their recoveries — a process that for some is expected to take months, even years.

"The care and recovery of our injured personnel, and the well-being of their families, remain our highest priorities," Canadian Forces officials said in a statement Saturday. "We continue to provide support to those affected and are deeply grateful to the medical teams caring for our personnel."
